title: Performance Reviews People Can Actually Use
summary: Most reviews arrive late and vague. How to build one from evidence, keep surprises out, check your own bias in calibration and write a growth plan people can act on.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
It's 5 p.m. and you have a half-written review open. There are notes from code reviews, a couple of project wins, one missed deadline, a Slack message from a product partner, and a fuzzy memory of a nasty incident where this engineer kept everyone on track. Filling in the form takes an hour. Making the review true takes a lot longer.

Reviews have a reputation problem. Gallup found that only 14% of employees strongly agree their performance reviews inspire them to improve (Gallup). That's a low bar, and most of the fixes are habits you can start this quarter.

Say what "solid" actually means

A review works when it connects everyday work to growth, trust and fair decisions. It fails when it turns into a yearly ceremony of vague adjectives. Nobody should have to decode whether "solid contributor" means on track for promotion, stuck, or a polite way of saying "disappointed." A useful review says what changed, what impact it had, which patterns need attention and what support comes next.

Vague praise also lands unevenly. Shelley Correll and Caroline Simard analyzed over 200 reviews at one large tech company and found that women's reviews contained vague praise more often than men's (57% versus 43%), while men's developmental feedback was more often tied to business outcomes (60% versus 40%) (Correll and Simard, HBR). "You had a great year" feels nice to read. It gives the person nothing to build a promotion case on.

Collect evidence all year

Memory makes a bad database. It overweights the last few weeks, the loud moments and whatever work the manager happened to see. The engineer who halved the alert noise, fixed onboarding or helped three teammates make better design calls can vanish if the system only remembers launches.

Keep a running doc per person and add to it as things happen: PRs, design notes, incidents, mentoring, production results, what partners say. Five minutes after each 1:1 is plenty. Write down context as well. Missing a target because the scope changed three times is a different story from missing it because nobody owned the work. Shipping a feature while carrying a migration and onboarding two new people is a different story from shipping it on a settled team. Context isn't an excuse. It keeps the evaluation honest.

No surprises at review time

The review should never be the first time someone hears important feedback. If an engineer learns in the formal review that their communication has been wearing on the team for six months, the process failed months ago. Gallup reports that nearly half of employees get feedback from their manager a few times a year or less, and says reviews work when they're consistent with frequent, honest feedback people have already heard (Gallup). Feedback close to the moment is something a person can practice on. The review then becomes a summary of a conversation that's already going.

Calibrate, starting with yourself

Calibration matters because people compare outcomes with each other. Two engineers with similar impact shouldn't end up with very different ratings because one manager writes more vividly or grades tougher.

The research here is humbling. In a study of 4,492 managers, each rated by two bosses, two peers and two direct reports, 62% of the variance in ratings came from the raters' own quirks of perception, and only 21% from actual performance (Mount, Scullen and Goff, as described by Buckingham and Goodall in HBR). A rating tells you a lot about whoever gave it.

So treat calibration as a habit of asking whether the evidence supports the conclusion, in the meeting and well before it. A few questions worth asking out loud:

  • Who's getting credit for glue work: unblocking teammates, reviewing designs, onboarding new hires? Tanya Reilly's talk "Being Glue" shows how often that work goes unrewarded when promotion time comes.
  • Who gets called "aggressive" for behavior someone else gets praised for? In Correll and Simard's data, 76% of references to being "too aggressive" showed up in women's reviews.
  • Whose confidence are we reading as competence?

Name the strengths, then one next step

Give strengths the same weight as gaps. They're more than padding around the criticism: they show where someone does the most good. Maybe they're great at untangling fuzzy requirements, teaching juniors, debugging incidents, simplifying code or building trust across teams. Name it precisely, so they can do it on purpose and the org can put them where it counts.

Keep the growth part small enough to act on. "Be more senior" helps nobody. "Lead one design review before implementation starts, write down the trade-offs and get feedback from the two teams it affects" gives someone a thing to practice. A good growth plan names a behavior, a situation where it'll come up, the support you'll give and how you'll both see progress. When I took over a delivery team after a CTO handover, I set up 1:1s with each person and a growth plan at 3, 6 and 12 months for each of them. Short horizons make a plan easy to check. Without that follow-through, the review becomes a document everyone politely forgets.

Be straight about pay and promotion

Pay and promotion make reviews emotionally heavy, and it's better to say so than pretend the review is only about development. People have rent, family plans and private worries riding on the outcome. Don't promise what you don't control. Explain the decision, the evidence behind it, the path forward and the constraints, clearly enough that nobody walks out with false hope or confusion they didn't need.

A good review is honest about the hard parts and makes them usable. It helps people see themselves more accurately, understand the setup they work in and pick their next few steps. The best review you ever got probably didn't feel like a form. It felt like someone had been paying attention.

Try this week

  • Start a running evidence doc for each person you'll review, and add one line after every 1:1.
  • Find one vague adjective in your last review ("solid," "great year") and replace it with what actually happened.
  • Before calibration, list the glue work each person did.
  • Write each growth goal as a behavior, a situation, the support you'll give and a check-in date.

Reviews only stay surprise-free if feedback flows in between. For that part, see giving constructive feedback.

faqs.q: What makes a performance review useful?
faqs.a: It connects everyday work to growth and fair decisions. It says what changed, what impact it had, which patterns need attention and what support comes next. Vague adjectives like "solid contributor" leave people guessing whether they're on track for promotion or falling behind.

faqs.q: How do I avoid recency bias in reviews?
faqs.a: Keep a running evidence doc for each person through the year: PRs, design notes, incidents, mentoring, production results and partner feedback. A few minutes after each 1:1 is enough. Note the context too, such as scope changes or a migration someone was carrying at the same time.

Ratings reflect the rater more than most people expect. In a study of 4,492 managers described in Harvard Business Review, 62% of the variance in ratings came from raters' own perceptions and only 21% from actual performance. Calibration checks whether the evidence supports each rating, including who gets credit for glue work.

faqs.q: Should feedback in the review ever be new?
faqs.a: Important feedback should never appear for the first time in a formal review. Gallup reports that nearly half of employees hear from their manager a few times a year or less, and that reviews work when they match frequent, honest feedback people have already received.

faqs.q: What does a good growth plan look like?
faqs.a: Small and specific. Name a behavior, a situation where it will come up, the support you'll give and how both of you will see progress. "Be more senior" helps nobody. "Lead one design review before implementation and get feedback from the two affected teams" gives someone something to practice.
